cbbb507690:
This chapter covers two ways the shape of the work, not the wording of the prompt, decides cost and quality.

The first half is the Message Batches API. Why is a deadline-tolerant workload priced at about half? What does the API guarantee, and what does it refuse to guarantee? We’ll cover how to choose between realtime and batch, and how to derive a submission cadence from an SLA. Then how to join, retry and chunk. And why you refine the prompt on a sample before you spend a day of queue time on the full set.

The second half is review architecture. Why can’t a model reliably review its own output in the context that produced it? What does an independent reviewer instance get, and what doesn’t it get? Why does one pass over a 14-file pull request go uneven? We’ll see how per-file passes plus an integration pass fix that, and how confidence is used to route findings rather than to prove them.

The two halves meet in section 21, where a multi-pass review runs as a pipeline of single-turn batch stages.
56e3e80dc2:
Both task statements reduce to two sentences.

Batch work is deadline-tolerant, single-turn work that you hand to the platform in bulk at about half price in exchange for giving up any latency guarantee, so you choose it by asking whether anyone is waiting, derive how often to submit from the SLA minus the 24-hour window, join results on custom_id because they arrive unordered, resubmit only the failures, and refine the prompt on a sample before paying for the whole set.

Review is only as independent as its context, so a model that reviews its own output in the same conversation inherits the reasoning that produced it, a single pass over a large change spreads attention thinly and unevenly, and the cure is to change the shape of the work: a fresh reviewer instance, per-file local passes, one cross-file integration pass, and confidence used to route findings to humans or to the pull request.
f04c892573:
Everything else in this chapter follows from those sentences.

Start with batch. The 50% price exists because the provider can schedule your work into slack capacity. That’s also why it can’t promise when the work will finish. Tool loops are banned inside a batch item because an item is one request and one response, and nobody is there to run your tool in the middle. Results come back unordered because the work is spread across machines and finishes in whatever order it finishes.

Now review. Self-review is weak because a language model’s next token depends on everything already in its context, including its own earlier justification. A large PR gets an uneven review because one prompt has one budget of attention for all of its content. And confidence is used for routing because a self-reported number is evidence of a certain kind, and nothing more.
8cb67a71f9:
The official exam guide states the following for the two task statements. This chapter teaches every point.

For 4.5, designing efficient batch processing strategies:

  • the Message Batches API gives about 50% cost savings, with a processing window of up to 24 hours and no guaranteed latency SLA;
  • it suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation), not blocking workflows (pre-merge checks);
  • it doesn’t support multi-turn tool calling within a single request, so you can’t execute tools mid-request and return results;
  • custom_id correlates each request with its response;
  • you calculate submission frequency from the SLA (for example, 4-hour submission windows to guarantee a 30-hour SLA, given the 24-hour processing window);
  • you handle batch failures by identifying failed documents by custom_id and resubmitting only those, with modifications such as chunking documents that exceeded context limits;
  • you refine prompts on a small sample set before processing the full set, to maximise first-pass success and cut iteration cost.

For 4.6, designing multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures:

  • self-review is limited because the model keeps the reasoning context that produced the output, which makes it less likely to question its own decisions;
  • an independent review instance without the generator’s reasoning is more effective than self-review instructions or extended thinking;
  • large reviews should be split into per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass, to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings;
  • verification passes can have the model self-report a confidence per finding, to enable calibrated review routing.
3f42a82c51:
A note on how this chapter relates to its neighbours.

  • Chapter 10 put Claude into CI and already made the realtime-versus-batch call for a pre-merge check. This chapter gives you the machinery behind that call.
  • Chapter 11 taught explicit criteria and few-shot examples. Those are what a reviewer instance needs in place of the generator’s reasoning.
  • Chapter 12 built the validation and retry-with-error-feedback loop for extraction. Section 10 and section 17 here show what that loop looks like when the retry can’t be a second turn.
  • Chapter 14 covers context preservation and escalation, including why self-reported confidence is a poor escalation trigger. That’s the other side of the routing use in section 20.

Sections are cross-referenced by number where it helps.
99cc050c0f:
Both halves of this chapter are old ideas in new clothes. The exam questions get easier once you see the clothes come off.

Batch processing is as old as business computing. Review as an independent act is older still. The only new thing is the worker: a language model whose price, latency and failure modes you have to learn.
e06f9ae969:
The first commercial computers ran one job at a time, and an operator fed them decks of punched cards. The machine was expensive, and a human at the console was slower than the machine. So the sensible way to run a workload was to collect jobs into a queue, run them back to back, and hand the output to the people who wanted it later.

IBM’s OS/360 (1960s) formalised this with Job Control Language. A job was a description of steps, datasets and resources, submitted to a scheduler that decided when to run it.

The word “batch” survived because the idea survived. You describe the work completely, up front. You don’t wait for it. And the system schedules it when and where it’s cheapest to run.
c1fe162b57:
Telecom is the industry where this matters most to you. A carrier produces a call detail record (CDR) for every call, text and data session.

For decades, the billing pipeline was a nightly or monthly batch. Mediation collected CDRs, a rating engine priced them, and a bill run produced invoices.

Then prepaid service arrived. The same pricing question now had to be answered while the call was in progress, because the network needed to know whether the subscriber still had balance. That required online charging: a realtime path with strict latency, a much higher cost per event, and a separate system.

Nobody ran prepaid authorisation through the monthly bill run. And nobody ran the monthly bill run as a hundred million synchronous charging requests. Task statement 4.5 asks you to apply the same split, for the same reasons, to Claude. The pre-merge check is online charging. The weekly technical-debt report is the bill run.
277d6e7ec4:
Google’s MapReduce paper (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) described a programming model for huge datasets. You split the data into independent chunks (map), run the chunks anywhere, and merge the partial results by key (reduce).

It matters here for two reasons. First, the execution engine was free to reschedule a failed chunk on a different machine without the caller noticing. That’s where the “resubmit only the failed items” discipline comes from. Second, the answer to a dataset too large for one worker was never a bigger worker. It was splitting by structure and merging by key, which is exactly how section 11 handles an oversized document.

In 2006 and 2009 the big cloud vendors began renting out computing capacity. In 2009 AWS introduced spot instances: spare capacity sold at a discount, on the condition that it can be reclaimed.

The economics are the same as the airline’s empty seat. Capacity that exists and sits idle earns nothing. So the seller will discount it to a buyer who accepts that the work may start late or be interrupted.
14bcf971c6:
Large language model inference has the same shape. Serving a model takes expensive accelerators, provisioned for peak interactive demand. Between peaks, they’re underused.

In 2024 the large providers began offering batch interfaces at roughly half the interactive price, in exchange for a completion window of up to a day. Anthropic’s Message Batches API arrived in the autumn of 2024. It has since grown to cover essentially the same request features as the Messages API (check the docs for the current list).

The contract hasn’t changed: a discount of about 50%, a window of up to 24 hours, no latency guarantee, and results matched to requests by an identifier you supply.
e7a0064c25:
The independent-review half has an equally long history.

Michael Fagan’s 1976 paper on design and code inspections at IBM described a formal process where the author doesn’t run the review. A moderator and several readers work from a checklist, and the author’s role is to answer questions. The reason was empirical. Authors are bad at finding their own defects. They aren’t careless. They read what they meant to write.

Banks encode the same insight as the four-eyes principle: the person who initiates a payment may not approve it. Modern pull-request review at large engineering organisations is a lighter version of the same rule. Bacchelli and Bird’s 2013 study of code review at Microsoft found that reviewers spend much of their effort understanding the change, and that finding defects is only one of several outcomes.

Two things hold across all of these. The reviewer must not share the author’s reasoning. And the reviewer needs an explicit definition of what to look for, because “look at this” produces a skim.
ae1ea971c9:
Once language models could write code and prose, the obvious next step was to have the model critique itself.

Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) used model-written critiques against a written set of principles during training. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) showed that a generate, critique, revise loop improved some tasks.

The follow-up work was more cautious. Huang et al. (2023, “Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet”) looked at models asked to revisit their own reasoning without an external signal, such as a test result or a ground-truth label. They often didn’t improve, and sometimes made correct answers worse. Work on LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) documented specific biases of model judges, including a tendency to prefer their own outputs and to be swayed by where content sits.

Separately, Liu et al. (2023) showed in “Lost in the Middle” that models use information in a long context less reliably when it sits in the middle than at the ends. That’s one concrete mechanism behind attention dilution.

Treat the specific numbers in those papers as belonging to their models and benchmarks. The direction of the findings is what carries over, and it matches the exam guide’s statements.
3526687711:
Start with the provider’s problem. A fleet of accelerators costs the same per hour, busy or idle.

Interactive traffic is bursty. It peaks in working hours and falls away at night. A provider that wants to answer interactive requests in a second has to hold enough capacity for the peak. So the average utilisation of that capacity sits well below one.

Now a request arrives saying “you may run this any time in the next 24 hours”. That’s worth much more to the provider than one that must start now, because it can be slotted into the gaps: the troughs between interactive peaks, the idle tail of a replica, a quiet region. The marginal cost of such work is low, and competitive pricing passes part of that saving on.

About half is the figure the platform advertises. Check the pricing page for the current number and the per-model token prices, because both change.
b3b5bcd195:
The price and the lack of an SLA are the same fact, seen from two sides.

If the provider promised that a batch would finish in ten minutes, it would have to reserve capacity for it. Reserved capacity is exactly what the discount removes. So the provider offers a generous bound (24 hours) instead of a typical time, and no latency guarantee at all.

In practice, the documentation notes that most batches finish well inside the window, often within an hour. But you can’t design against “most”. A system that only works if the batch finishes in an hour will miss its commitment one day in a hundred. And it’ll do so on the day the platform is busiest, which is likely your busiest day too.
d72b0d2bcf:
Three practical consequences follow, and the exam probes all three.

First, the discount only applies to work whose result nobody is waiting for. If a developer, a customer or a downstream pipeline step blocks on the answer, the missing latency guarantee is a defect, not a trade-off.

Second, the price is per request, however it’s submitted. So there’s no benefit to batching a handful of items. The saving is proportional to volume, while the extra complexity of polling, joining and retrying is a fixed cost.

Third, the platform is free to schedule items in any order and on any machine. Nothing about the order of results, or even the order of completion, is promised. You get a bag of results keyed by an identifier, and your code owns the bookkeeping.

The Spring analogy is an @Async method returning a CompletableFuture, compared with a Spring Batch job. The first gets the answer to a caller who is waiting. The second gives you chunked, restartable processing of a large input, where you care about throughput and completeness, not the latency of any one item.
9ed75d9da7:
Before the design questions, look at the bytes. You create a batch with one HTTP request whose body is a list of items. Each item has the identifier you choose and the params of an ordinary Messages API request.

Nothing about the params is special. Same model, same system prompt, same tool definitions, same tool_choice as you’d use with messages.create.

This is deliberate, and it has a useful consequence. A prompt you debugged in realtime on a few examples works in a batch unchanged. That’s what makes the sample-first workflow of section 12 possible. (Companion: 01_batch_request_shape.py.)
4f839cf82f:
Three things in that request make up the whole API surface you need to design around.

custom_id is yours, and it must be unique within the batch. The documented pattern at the time of writing is one to 64 characters from letters, digits, underscore and hyphen. The companion fake enforces the same pattern and rejects the whole submission on a violation. So build identifiers from a safe alphabet (check the docs for the current rule).

params is validated at submission for shape. But a problem inside one item’s content, such as a prompt that exceeds the context window, is reported later as that item’s own error. It doesn’t fail the batch. Example 08 shows this.

And the request says nothing about when you want the answer, because there’s nothing to set. You get the platform’s best effort inside the window.
d382d956f8:
The batch object is a status record. Nothing in it is a result.

processing_status is in_progress while any item is still being worked. It’s canceling if you asked to cancel and the cancellation is still in flight. It’s ended once every item has reached a final state.

request_counts is the tally. It tells you how many items are still processing and how many ended each way, which is what a monitoring dashboard should chart. The expires_at field is the 24-hour mark. Items still unprocessed at that time end as expired.

Treat the status as the only thing you poll. Fetching results before the batch has ended isn’t how the API is meant to be used, and the companion fake refuses it with a 400.
fc57acd442:
Results come back as JSON Lines, one object per item. The stream order has nothing to do with the order you sent. In the example above, inv00017 comes before inv00003. The only reliable key is custom_id.

A succeeded result carries a normal Messages API message. You parse it exactly as you parse a realtime response: here, by finding the tool_use block and reading its input.

The Python SDK hides the HTTP behind client.messages.batches.create(requests=[...]), .retrieve(batch_id), .results(batch_id) (an iterator over the stream), .cancel(batch_id) and .list().

Companion example 02 runs this whole cycle against the fake on a virtual clock, so a 3-hour batch takes milliseconds. It asserts that the order received differs from the order sent.
87779306e6:
The lifecycle has two levels, and exam-grade understanding means keeping them apart. The batch has a status. Each item has a result type. Batch status tells you whether to keep waiting. Item result type tells you what to do about each item.

Mixing them up produces the commonest bug in first-time batch code: treating “the batch ended” as “the batch succeeded”.

A batch with processing_status: ended can contain any mix of successes, errors, expirations and cancellations. A status of ended with 8% errored items is the normal, expected outcome of a large run. It isn’t an exception.
4d2486718e:
Several facts from the documentation shape the design. They’re the kind that drift, so each one is flagged for a recheck.

  • A batch is limited in item count and in total size. At the time of writing, the documentation states 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first (check the docs). So a 2-million-document backlog becomes twenty or more batches, and the cadence maths of section 08 applies to each.
  • Results are kept for a limited period measured from creation, documented as 29 days at the time of writing. A pipeline must download and persist results into your own store as soon as the batch ends. Don’t treat the platform as the archive.
  • Errored, expired and cancelled items are documented as not billed. That’s why a retry round only costs the retried items. Check the docs for the exact billing statement.
  • Rate limits apply both to the HTTP calls you make against the Batches endpoints and to the number of requests waiting in queue. The documentation points to the rate-limits page instead of stating numbers.
  • And max_tokens must be at least 1 for each item.
1198707d3d:
A family of features works in a batch exactly as in realtime, and the list is longer than people expect. System prompts, vision inputs, tool definitions with forced tool use (the extraction pattern of Chapter 12), extended thinking, and prompt caching (section 13) are all documented as supported. Streaming isn’t: an item returns a complete message.

That list changes, so the reliable test is the one the exam guide uses. A feature is available inside a batch item if it can happen within one request-and-response exchange. It isn’t if it needs your code to run between two model turns.
948707781c:
The exam guide states this limit as a flat rule. The Batches API doesn’t support multi-turn tool calling within a single request, so you can’t execute tools mid-request and return results.

The mechanism is easy to see once you recall Chapter 1. An agentic loop is your code calling the model, reading stop_reason: "tool_use", running the tool, appending a tool_result, and calling again. The tool runs in your process, against your systems, with your credentials.

A batch item is a single request that goes into a queue and comes out as a single response hours later. When the model answers with a tool_use block, the item is finished. The platform has produced the one response it owes you, and nobody is there to run lookup_order and send the result back.

So an item that needs a tool result before it can finish can’t finish inside the batch. (Companion: 03_no_multiturn_in_batch.py.)
b4fd86071a:
Be careful about two things here. Read loosely, the exam and the documentation can sound like they disagree.

First, the limit concerns your client-side tools, the ones whose results only your code can supply. A batch item can legitimately contain a multi-message history: for example, a previous assistant turn and a tool result you already have, as in item 2 above. The documentation also lists support for features such as extended thinking, and for tools the platform itself runs server-side (check the docs for the current list of server tools in batches, and for how pause_turn is handled). What an item can’t do is pause mid-way and wait for your code.

Second, you can build a multi-stage workflow out of several batches. Each stage is a separate batch, and you run the tools between them. That works. But each stage waits for its own window, so a loop of five tool calls costs up to five windows. For a nightly job that may be fine. For anything a person is waiting for, it isn’t.
59b44979ca:
The practical rule, which the next section’s decision procedure builds on, is to look at what each item must do.

A single-turn item is a classification, an extraction with a forced tool, a summarisation, a scored review of a provided diff, a translation, or an embedding-preparation rewrite. All of those can be batched.

An item that must look something up, search, call an API, read a file the model chooses, or take an action is an agent. Agents run in the realtime loop of Chapter 1, or in the Agent SDK.

There’s a middle path when the lookups are predictable. Do them yourself before building the batch, and put the data into the prompt. Say a nightly job scores 30,000 support tickets. It can fetch each ticket’s order history in a pre-processing step and embed it, instead of giving the model a lookup_order tool. That turns an agent into a single-turn item. The price is deciding up front what the model needs.
717dff19cc:
The central design skill of 4.5 isn’t knowing the API. It’s deciding which workloads belong on it.

Five questions settle it, asked in order. The order matters, because the first yes to a blocking question ends the discussion. (Companion: 04_sync_vs_batch_router.py, which encodes the procedure and tests it on eight workloads.)
2ac7fffadc: Is anything blocked waiting for this result? A developer watching a merge button, a customer in a chat, a pipeline stage that gates a release. If yes, go realtime, whatever the price. Batch has no latency guarantee, and a blocked person is a latency requirement.
688513ae59: Does each item need client-side tool results in the middle? If yes, the item is an agent. It belongs on the realtime loop, or has to be re-expressed as staged batches (section 06) or as a single-turn item with the data pre-fetched.
1b4a039aa7: Is there a deadline that the 24-hour window can meet? Take the business SLA, minus the 24-hour window, minus your own post-processing. What’s left must allow a submission cadence you can run (section 08). If the SLA is shorter than the window, batch can’t meet it.
d3fdbc2781: Is the prompt validated? A batch with a flawed prompt costs the same as a good one, and you find out a day later. Refine on a sample first (section 12).
d80f5abcf3:
The exam’s CI scenario gives you exactly two jobs and asks you to place them. Job one reviews every pull request before merge, and developers wait for it. Job two generates a weekly technical-debt report across all repositories, and no one waits for it. Finance asks to cut spend.

The tempting answer is to move both to batch, for 50% off both. The correct answer is to move only job two.

Job one fails question one. A blocked developer is a latency requirement. A batch that takes four hours, or a day, turns every pull request into a next-day merge.

Companion example 11 simulates the broken design. It runs batch durations of 0.4, 2 and 23.5 hours against a ten-minute developer budget, and reports BLOCKED at all three, even the optimistic one. The 23.5-hour row makes the point: “most batches finish within an hour” is a typical case, and a workflow that depends on the typical case is a workflow with an outage rate.
f25734e122:
Chapter 10 section 16 made the same call from the CI side, and shows where each job runs: claude -p in a pipeline step for the blocking check, and a scheduled job that builds a batch for the nightly report.

The two chapters agree, and the exam draws on both. A question that presents a CI pipeline with a blocking check and an overnight job is always 4.5. The answer is always that only the overnight job moves.
eec45876d7:
Three less obvious errors deserve names, because each has shown up in exam distractors.

A job that isn’t urgent isn’t necessarily batchable. A research agent that runs overnight still needs a tool loop, and putting it in a batch fails at the first tool_use.

A job that’s batchable isn’t necessarily worth batching. If you process a few hundred items a month, the discount saves cents. Meanwhile the polling, join and retry code adds an operational surface that someone has to own.

And a batch isn’t a place to experiment. A batch has no latency guarantee, so every iteration of a flawed prompt costs a day. An iteration on the full set is also a full-price mistake (albeit at half price). The sample step of section 12 exists to move experimentation to the realtime API, where an iteration takes seconds.
865e4b9ff9:
The exam guide gives one worked example and expects you to generalise it: a 4-hour submission window guarantees a 30-hour SLA, given the 24-hour processing window.

Don’t memorise it. Derive it. The derivation also tells you how to handle post-processing time, and why “once a day” is a trap. (Companion: 05_sla_math.py.)
2bc4d079a3:
Say the business promises that a document arriving at time t has its result available by t + SLA. You don’t send each document the moment it arrives. You collect documents and submit a batch every I hours (the submission interval).

Consider the worst-case document. It arrives just after a submission, so it waits almost a full interval I for the next batch to go out. Then the batch takes up to 24 hours. Then you spend some time P on your own post-processing: downloading, validating, loading into a database.

The worst-case time from arrival to usable result is therefore I + 24 + P. The SLA holds for every document if and only if that worst case is no larger than the SLA:
ab704d4eb3:
The exam’s own example says “4-hour submission windows to guarantee 30-hour SLA”. Our derivation gives a maximum interval of 6 hours for a 30-hour SLA. So a 4-hour interval satisfies it, with two hours of slack.

Both are right. The formula gives the longest permissible interval. A real schedule picks a comfortable value below it, because the 24 hours is a bound for the batch alone. Your own steps (building the batch, queueing behind the previous one, retrying failures) take time too.

When a question asks “what is the maximum”, apply the formula. When it offers a list of intervals and asks which one guarantees the SLA, pick any at or below the formula’s result. If the guide’s value is among the options, prefer it.
e40da990fa:
Example 05 also simulates it, instead of trusting the algebra. Documents arrive every six minutes for 96 hours, batches go out every I hours, and each batch is assumed to take the full 24 hours.

The output is submit every 6 h -> worst-case end-to-end 30.0 h (meets a 30 h SLA: True), every 12 h -> 36.0 h (False), every 24 h -> 48.0 h (False).

The last line is the trap behind the exam’s “submit once a day” distractor. A nightly cron that sends everything that piled up during the day is the natural design. And it quietly gives you an effective 48-hour worst case.
65e05dc993:
The formula sets a floor on the cadence. A few real-world effects push you to submit more often than it requires.

Retries consume window. Say a batch has 3% expired items and you resubmit them. The second round starts after the first has ended, so the true worst case for a retried item is I + 24 + 24 + P. If the SLA must hold for retried items too, either halve your budget (SLA - 48 h - P), or accept that a small, known fraction may exceed it and escalate those.

Batch size limits split a large day into several batches, each with its own window. But they run in parallel, so the formula still applies per batch.

Load stretches the tail. The docs note that demand can slow processing and increase expirations. Leave headroom instead of running at the formula’s limit.
a1e3456623:
There’s also a design choice hiding in the formula: you can trade submission frequency against batch size.

Submitting every 2 hours instead of every 6 means three times as many, smaller batches. That costs nothing extra in tokens, since price is per request, not per batch. But it triples the number of status polls and result downloads. So shorter intervals are cheap in dollars, and cost only operational complexity.

The usual compromise is to pick the largest convenient interval at or below the limit, such as the guide’s 4 hours for a 30-hour SLA.
378cf39ce4:
Two points about that code.

The check in the static block is the SLA formula as an invariant. A configuration change that stretches the interval fails the deployment, instead of failing the commitment a month later.

And the mapping from custom_id back to your own rows lives in your database. It isn’t reconstructed from the identifier alone. The identifier is a key, not a data store.
20ba9f02e1:
Every batch correlation problem comes down to one fact. Results arrive in an order unrelated to the order of submission. So the identifier on each item is the only thing that ties a result to whatever produced it.

The exam asks this directly (“how do you match results to requests?”). The answer is always custom_id, never position.

This isn’t the API being quirky. Items are spread across workers and finish at different times. An API that returned them in order would have to hold the fastest results until the slowest arrived. Unordered delivery is a consequence of parallelism.
2e553b7029:
A good custom_id does three jobs. Design it deliberately, and you save hours later.

  • It must be unique within the batch, or the submission is rejected.
  • It must be meaningful, so you can route a result without a lookup: the document or ticket id, plus enough context to know which question was asked.
  • It should be version-tagged. When you re-run the corpus with an improved prompt, you can then tell old results from new in your store, and compare them.

The companion library uses {doc_id}__{prompt_version}, such as inv00017__v2. Why the double underscore? The allowed alphabet excludes dots, colons and slashes. A sloppy separator is an easy way to hit the character rule on the first run.
4faf7e0f7c:
The classic bug is to assume the results stream is in request order, and zip the two lists.

It works on a three-item test, where the platform happens to return them in order. Then it silently corrupts a production run. Nothing raises. A total from one invoice simply gets stored against another. Companion example 12 reproduces it with 25 invoices, and prints how many results land on the wrong record.
d90834a426:
Notice the second half of the fixed version. Look up each expected identifier, and treat a missing key as an error. That gives you a completeness check for free.

After joining, the set of identifiers you sent should equal the set of results you received. Any difference is either a bug in your pipeline or an item that never reached a final state. Example 02 asserts sorted(sent) == sorted(received) before it does anything else with the data.
182d4ca049:
Large runs fail in pieces. In a 50,000-item batch, expect a few hundred items to come back errored or expired. The exam asks what to do about them.

The wrong answers are the instructive ones.

  • Resubmitting the whole batch pays again for every item that already succeeded (documented as billed on success). It also risks two different results for the same document in your store.
  • Ignoring the failures leaves silent gaps in the output.
  • Retrying the failures unchanged loops forever on items that fail for a reason you could have fixed.

The right answer has three parts. Identify the failed items by custom_id. Classify each failure as retry-as-is or fix-first. Then resubmit only those, with whatever modification the cause requires. (Companion: 06_failure_by_custom_id.py.)
70793b2cbc:
A failed item belongs in one of two bins, and the item’s own result tells you which.

Some items failed through nothing in the request: an expired or canceled item, or an errored item with a server-side error type (api_error, overloaded_error). The platform just didn’t finish them. Resubmit them unchanged.

An errored item with invalid_request_error failed because of the request itself. The prompt exceeded the context window, a parameter was out of range, or a message was malformed. It’ll fail again for the same reason, so a blind retry wastes a window. Fix the cause first.

The documentation’s own results example makes the same split. Validation errors mean “fix the request body before resending”. Server errors “can retry directly”.
df52a12c1e: Now the trace from example 06. Try to predict it before you read it. The run submits 40 invoices. Three are made to expire on the first attempt, and two to hit a server error. One has max_tokens: 0, which is malformed.
59ad2860c6:
The last assertion is the one that makes the point. The fake records how many times each custom_id was processed, and the test requires that none of the 34 successes ran a second time.

The tally for the whole job is 40 items in the first batch and 6 in the second. That’s 46 item-processings for 40 documents. Resubmitting everything would have been 80.

Example 07 prices the difference on 100 invoices with 5 failures. Resubmitting everything cost $0.2109, against $0.1081 for failures only: a 95% overspend. The token prices in the fake are illustrative. The ratio is the point.
478a9b6ae2:
The third failure mode is the one the API can’t report. An item can succeed at the API level and still produce an unusable result. Maybe the model returned a tool_use block with a null total, because the document used a layout the prompt didn’t cover. Maybe a date came back in the wrong format. Maybe it stopped on max_tokens with a truncated block.

Chapter 12 separated three levels of correctness: syntax (guaranteed by forced tool use), schema (mostly guaranteed) and semantics (never guaranteed). That separation applies unchanged to batch results. The semantic check belongs in your collection step, after the join, as a pure function of the record.

Records that fail it go into the next batch as failures, with one difference from Chapter 12. In realtime, a validation failure is retried by appending the error to the conversation, as a second turn. Batch has no second turn. So the retry is a new single-turn item whose user message contains the document, the previous output and the validation errors.

Example 17 does exactly that. Round one, with a prompt that lacks the legacy-layout rule, yields 6 semantically invalid records out of 30. Round two resubmits only those six, with their errors, and all validate. The retry costs 20% of round one, and its latency is a second window.
829775d160: This is also why you validate and sample before the full run. If the prompt has a systematic gap, 20% of the corpus fails validation, and the cleanup costs a second window and 20% more spend. Section 12 shows how a small sample finds the gap for the price of a few realtime calls.
b06b8db81c:
The exam guide names one specific modification for resubmitted failures: chunking documents that exceeded context limits.

The failure is simple. An item whose prompt is larger than the model’s context window can’t be processed. It’s reported as that item’s own invalid_request_error (“prompt is too long”) when the batch ends, not when you submit it.

That detail matters for planning. You can’t rely on the submission call to catch oversized documents. So either measure token counts before building the batch, or expect a fix-first failure bucket and handle it.

Resubmitting the same document unchanged fails identically. The remedy isn’t a larger model or a lower max_tokens. Split the document, process the pieces as separate items, and merge. (Companion: 08_chunking_oversized.py.)
3ec973ebc9:
Where you cut decides the quality of the result.

Arbitrary byte or token boundaries split a sentence, a table row or an invoice line in half. The model then sees a fragment it can’t interpret. Cut on structure instead: chapter or section headings in a report, page boundaries in a scanned contract, line items in a statement, file boundaries in a repository, speaker turns in a transcript.

Sometimes the structure has no natural boundary at a convenient size. Then cut at the nearest structural boundary below the limit, and add a short overlap of the preceding items. A fact that straddles the cut then appears whole in at least one chunk.

Overlap has a cost. The overlapped content is processed twice, and any value extracted from it can be double-counted when you merge. That’s why the merge step must be keyed.
06992120a6:
Each chunk becomes its own batch item, with a custom_id that records which chunk it is (stmt-acme9__c003of008). Each item returns structured output keyed by something stable within the document, such as the line id.

The merge is a reduce step in the MapReduce sense. Group by document id, then union the per-chunk results keyed by the item id, so the overlapped lines collapse into one. Example 08 demonstrates both the failure and the fix, with a 400-line statement and a deliberately small context limit.
